rationale: ZILRETTA clearly beat saline at Week 12 in the large knee pivotal (p<0.0001), but that trial had about 160 patients per arm. This trial has about 100 versus 50, so if the knee effect (roughly 1 point on the NRS, effect size about 0.4) carries over, power is only around 60–70%. Shoulder OA is untested for efficacy and intra-articular steroid evidence in the shoulder is thin. The looser pain entry criterion (≥4) and typically large saline placebo responses add risk, partly offset by placebo-response-reduction training. Signs of trouble include a dropped TCA-IR arm, a timeline-related impairment and the vague interim analysis, so I put this near a coin flip.

Plasma-derived C1-INH at 20 IU/kg against placebo is a well-proven approach: IMPACT-1 (Berinert) with the same n≈124 and dose met its time-to-relief endpoint, and Cinryze and Ruconest also succeeded. OCTA-C1-INH is essentially a biosimilar-like plasma concentrate, so its efficacy should be similar. Risks include the stricter three-consecutive-rating relief definition, a sizable placebo response, heterogeneous multinational sites that may add noise, and recruitment slippage that could shrink the blinded sample. A high but not near-certain probability seems appropriate.

Every placebo-controlled IGF-1R antibody trial in active TED I know of has met the proptosis responder endpoint by wide margins, with placebo responses of roughly 4–18% against active responses of 50–85%. MHB018A's Phase 1/2 showed an 81% proptosis response at Week 12 at the chosen 450 mg dose, and with 108 patients the trial has ample power for even a modest class effect. The remaining risk comes from a novel subcutaneous antibody whose Week 24 durability and placebo-controlled effect have not been shown, plus the single-site design and no DMC. No topline result for this trial has been found, although the sponsor's press release title mentioning 'Phase III results' is somewhat ambiguous.

Solriamfetol has consistently produced large MWT gains versus placebo in narcolepsy and OSA, and a small 4-week SWD RCT showed a 9.4-minute MWT benefit (P<0.001), so the first-listed MWT endpoint is very likely to succeed with roughly 150 per arm. The main risks are the co-primary CGI-S endpoint, a heterogeneous real-world SWD population, the 12-week duration, and higher placebo response in subjective measures. Modafinil and armodafinil did succeed on similar endpoints in SWD. The unexplained timeline slip adds slight uncertainty, but overall success is likely.

MT1013 is an IV calcimimetic-type agent whose Phase II iPTH response rates (about 74–77% reaching >50% reduction) roughly matched etelcalcetide. Etelcalcetide itself beat oral cinacalcet head-to-head on both >30% and >50% iPTH reduction, partly because in-clinic IV dosing removes adherence problems, and this trial (n≈435) is well sized for a similar effect. The design is unstated; if it tests non-inferiority, success is very likely, while superiority on the >50% endpoint is plausible but less certain. No results have been reported and the trial remains blinded, so I put the probability at about 0.75.

No neonatal HIE adjunct to cooling has yet shown a significant benefit on MRI injury scores; erythropoietin's small phase 2 MRI signal did not hold up in HEAL. RLS-0071 is a novel anti-inflammatory peptide with only preclinical and PK support, and the phase 2 portion now targets about 70 infants split across moderate and severe HIE and two dose levels, so it is likely underpowered for a continuous Weeke score. The shifting endpoints and slipping timelines add uncertainty, though a continuous MRI score and a possible favorable sponsor analysis leave some chance of a nominal win.

The DPP1 mechanism is validated in bronchiectasis: brensocatib's large ASPEN phase 3 succeeded, with roughly a 20% reduction in exacerbation rate, and HSK31858's own phase 2 showed a strong, highly significant reduction (IRR 0.41 at 40 mg) in a Chinese population similar to this one. The phase 2 effect is likely inflated, but with about 700 patients, 52 weeks of follow-up, 2:1 randomization and a requirement of at least 2 prior exacerbations, the trial should still be reasonably powered for a 25–30% reduction. The main risks are regression of the effect toward brensocatib-like sizes, a high placebo response, and an assumed effect size that is not disclosed; even so, phase 3 success after strong phase 2 data with a validated mechanism is likely.

TQB3616 (culmerciclib) is a CDK4-biased inhibitor with strong PFS benefit in advanced HR+/HER2− disease, and the two CDK4/6 inhibitors with similar profiles (abemaciclib, ribociclib) met iDFS in adjuvant phase 3 trials, while palbociclib failed twice. This trial is double-blind and reasonably sized (n≈1946, 2:1), but the eligibility criteria do not clearly restrict to high-risk patients, and follow-up is short (start 2023, primary completion 2026-12), so a low event count could leave it underpowered. Chinese sponsors often have favorable topline readouts, but the adjuvant CDK4/6 track record is roughly 50/50, so I put the probability slightly above even.

The FDA asked Karyopharm to withdraw the DLBCL indication in March 2026 because the company could not complete this confirmatory trial, and the company has said it will stop DLBCL development costs. That makes a completed, positive Phase 3 PFS readout very unlikely. The underlying efficacy case was also modest: SADAL showed 29% ORR single-arm, there are no randomized data for adding selinexor to R-GDP, and the related endometrial Phase 3 narrowly missed on PFS. The remaining probability mainly covers the chance that some prespecified analysis, such as the Phase 2 ORR, comes out positive, or that a truncated analysis is reported favorably.

This is a non-inferiority trial with a 5-point margin and about 440 patients per arm, so the lower confidence bound sits roughly 2.5 points below the observed difference. The sister trial C-BEYOND, with the same design and comparator, met non-inferiority in mITT (93.9% vs 94.8%), and C-FORWARD's per-protocol primary analysis should push both arms higher and reduce discontinuation noise. The main risks are a genotype mix richer in GT3 and GT4 (Pakistan, India, Egypt), where BEM/RZR's 8-week regimen and its small Phase 2 GT3 dataset are less proven, and a modest timeline slip. Overall success looks likely but not certain.

The design mirrors pafolacianine's ELUCIDATE: the primary endpoint is a CSE proportion in the NIR arm tested against a fixed low threshold (likely about 10%), and the small randomized control arm exists mainly to preserve blinding. Phase 2b VISUALIZE produced about a 40–45% CSE rate with a lower 95% bound of 34%, far above a 10% null, and pafolacianine succeeded on a near-identical design. The main risks are a stricter prespecified threshold than the 10% used before, a CSE definition narrower than phase 2b's (margins excluded), lower yield at the untested 96-hour dosing window, or a shift to more experienced surgeons. Even so, the bar looks comfortably clearable with about 115 evaluable patients.

Iza-bren has already beaten chemotherapy on OS in randomized Chinese Phase 3 trials in TNBC and ESCC, and it met PFS at interim in EGFR-mutant NSCLC. Its single-arm ORR of roughly 30–45% in EGFR-wild-type disease is well above docetaxel's ~13%, and 698 patients should give good power for a modest OS hazard ratio. Against that, OS versus docetaxel after immunotherapy and platinum has defeated similar ADCs (Dato-DXd in TROPION-Lung01, HER3-DXd in HERTHENA-Lung02). Toxicity and the heterogeneous wild-type population (including squamous) could also dilute the survival gain. Balancing the drug's track record and a China-only setting with limited crossover against this historically hard endpoint, I put success slightly above even.

Relutrigine showed large, highly significant placebo-adjusted seizure reductions in EMBOLD (53%, p<0.0002), but only in SCN2A/SCN8A gain-of-function patients, whose disease biology suits a sodium-channel blocker. EMERALD enrolls a broad, heterogeneous DEE population, where the effect is likely diluted and some genotypes may respond poorly. Its sample size of about 160–200 still gives reasonable power for a moderate effect on motor seizure frequency. Praxis's recent misses with vormatrigine and ulixacaltamide, plus the lack of precedent for sodium-channel drugs in broad DEE, temper my confidence, so I put success moderately above even.

This is a descriptive phase 3a safety study of GSK's VNS varicella vaccine against Varivax, with no prespecified hypothesis test, so 'meeting the endpoint' in practice means the sponsor reports an acceptable, comparable safety profile. In phase 2, adverse event rates were similar to Varivax and seroresponse was high, and GSK has a long track record with Oka-strain vaccines. Descriptive safety trials almost always end with a 'well tolerated, comparable to control' topline. The remaining risk is an unexpected rash or fever signal, or ambiguity in how such a descriptive trial is scored.

Iltamiocel's FI evidence is uncontrolled (Phase 1/2, roughly 54% with ≥50% reduction), and FI episode-frequency endpoints are known for large placebo and regression-to-the-mean responses, as seen with bulking agents and sham-controlled trials. The same autologous muscle-derived cell product failed its randomized placebo-controlled Phase 3 in stress urinary incontinence (52% vs 53.6%), a close mechanistic analogue. Enrollment of about 100–200 with a continuous frequency endpoint gives some power, but the base rate for a cell therapy beating vehicle placebo here is low.

No drug has yet shown a benefit on hard clinical outcomes in compensated NASH cirrhosis, and event-driven trials in this population struggle with low placebo event rates (about 2–3% per year), long timelines and dilution from dropout and background therapy. Resmetirom is a proven antifibrotic in F2–F3 NASH, and open-label F4 data show liver-stiffness reductions and some regression, which gives it a better rationale than most entrants. However, histologic and stiffness gains in cirrhosis have not reliably translated into fewer decompensation events, and the 3:1 randomization limits placebo events. Weighing a credible mechanism against a historically very hard endpoint, I put success somewhat below even odds.

WD-890 appears to be an oral TYK2-type inhibitor (it suppressed IL-17 and IFN-γ in an IL-23 mouse model), a mechanism already validated against placebo in psoriasis by deucravacitinib and zasocitinib. The sponsor's move to Phase 3 suggests its Phase 2 dose-ranging data were encouraging. Against placebo with sPGA 0/1 and PASI 75 at week 16 and about 375 patients, the trial has ample power even for a modest effect. The main risks are a weak small Chinese sponsor with an undisclosed Phase 2, possible underdosing, and execution or record issues such as a single site and stale dates.

Adjuvant immunotherapy add-ons to gemcitabine in resected pancreatic cancer have a poor record (GI-4000, algenpantucel-L, erlotinib/sorafenib in CONKO-005/006), and this trial has no randomized pancreatic data behind it, only preclinical and retrospective signals. The HCC adjuvant RFS success shows Immuncell-LC can reduce recurrence, and the open-label design against a weak gemcitabine-only control helps somewhat. Still, pancreatic cancer's immunosuppressive biology and early systemic relapse make a meaningful RFS benefit unlikely, and with 408 patients only a moderate hazard ratio would reach significance. The record has not been updated since 2021 and no result is public, so recruitment may be slow and the readout delayed.

vYF is a Vero-cell-derived 17D vaccine that showed near-identical day-29 seroconversion to YF-VAX in adults (99.7% vs 99.4%), so non-inferiority against licensed 17D comparators should be likely, and the same vYF arm is compared with both Stamaril and YF-VAX. Pediatric seroconversion is lower and more variable, which shrinks the margin of safety. There are four co-primary comparisons across two age groups, and if all must pass, joint risk rises, though the large sample (about 600 per vYF age group) gives good power. Sanofi runs this trial as a regulatory-grade effort, and non-inferiority trials of near-copy live vaccines usually succeed.

KarXT is proven in schizophrenia, and xanomeline monotherapy showed dose-dependent reductions in hallucinations and delusions in Alzheimer's disease, so the mechanism is plausible here, but no randomized data on this endpoint exist yet. Psychosis trials in Alzheimer's disease have a poor record: placebo responses on NPI-type scales are high, pimavanserin missed in an AD-only trial and in its AD subgroup, and atypical antipsychotics show only small effects. The add-on schizophrenia trial missed, and slow enrollment amid eligibility stringency plus site irregularities at a sister trial add execution risk. With about 400 patients, the trial is adequately powered for a modest effect, so a forecast near 45% balances the drug's mechanistic promise against the field's high failure rate.

Rimegepant is a proven oral gepant with demonstrated preventive efficacy in episodic migraine, and the same-class atogepant LUNA trial, using an identical 7-day perimenstrual regimen, met its primary endpoint with a highly significant 0.8-day placebo-adjusted reduction. The roughly 723 participants across four arms give about 180 per arm, adequate power for a similar effect. Risks are rimegepant's weaker preventive potency than atogepant (its plasma half-life of about 11 h makes once-daily dosing modest), the small absolute benefit in a 5-day window, high placebo responses, and unclear multiplicity handling across two rimegepant arms. The status and timeline inconsistency suggests the trial may still be ongoing.

Navenibart is a long-acting anti-plasma-kallikrein antibody, the same validated mechanism as lanadelumab, and its open-label data showed 84–95% attack reductions. Every placebo-controlled HAE prophylaxis trial on attack rate has succeeded, usually with p<0.001. With about 145 adults across three active arms and placebo, and placebo attack rates near 2 per month, the trial is well powered even for modest effects. The main risks are operational or dosing problems, especially with the every-6-month regimen, but only one arm needs to win.

This is a small (150-patient) single-dose Phase III of an undisclosed chemoneurolytic injection against intra-articular/perineural saline in US knee OA, a setting with very high placebo response and frequent late-stage failures. The Phase II COMPASS results were never published with effect sizes. Still, the sponsor advanced to Phase III with the same investigators, and enrollment uses a diagnostic nerve-block responder enrichment, which plausibly raises the effect size. Given the modest sample, the shifted endpoint (pain while walking) and the base rate for OA pain injectables, success is somewhat less likely than not.

Topical add-on drugs for venous leg ulcers have a poor Phase 3 track record (HP802-247, LL-37 and others failed), and TR987's earlier evidence is weak: the Phase 2b primary result was never clearly reported, and the support is a post hoc pooled wound-area analysis with p=0.03 rather than complete closure. Compression standard of care produces substantial closure rates, so a modest add-on effect is hard to show on a binary closure endpoint. The small sponsor reports slow recruitment (~100 of 312 randomized by mid-2026), has de-prioritised one of its two studies, and is talking about a device pathway that may affect the drug trial, all of which make an adequately powered positive result less likely. Counting the real chance that the trial stops or finishes underpowered, the probability of a significant primary result is low.

Ivonescimab adds a VEGF-blocking component, and bevacizumab plus paclitaxel reliably improved PFS in metastatic breast cancer (E2100). That makes a PFS gain over nab-paclitaxel alone plausible even in a largely PD-L1-negative population, where PD-1 agents alone have failed. Phase 2 TNBC data (ORR 80%, median PFS about 9.3 months, including CPS <10) look strong against an expected control median of about 5 months, and Akeso's China-only placebo-controlled phase 3s have a strong record of hitting PFS, with 416 patients adequate for a hazard ratio around 0.65. Risks are the small uncontrolled phase 2, the PD-L1-negative biology, and possible attenuation under independent central review; no result is public yet.

This is an equivalence trial of a pembrolizumab biosimilar against Keytruda, and biosimilar equivalence trials on ORR usually succeed. The closest analogue, Samsung Bioepis SB27 in the same setting, met its margin with 555 patients, and this trial is larger at 808, which narrows the confidence interval. The main risks are that Qilu's margin may be tighter than SB27's, that random ORR variation could push the interval outside it (SB27's point estimate was 0.91), and that some uncertainty about execution and possible delays remains. Overall the probability of meeting the equivalence margin is high but not certain.

This is essentially a NETTER-1-style design (177Lu-SSA plus standard octreotide LAR vs high-dose octreotide LAR) in SSTR-positive G1–G2 GEP-NETs. Every comparable randomized trial of this mechanism gave very large PFS effects: NETTER-1 HR 0.18, the Chinese XT-XTR008 trial HR 0.06, and NETTER-2 in pNET HR 0.34. With about 220 patients and a weak control arm, power is very high even if the effect is attenuated. The main risks are operational: only two sites, still recruiting near the planned completion date, and a possible delay or early termination, which leaves a residual chance of failure.

Empagliflozin is a proven SGLT2 inhibitor that has consistently lowered HbA1c by about 0.6–0.8% versus placebo as add-on therapy, including Korean triple-therapy trials on metformin plus a DPP-4 inhibitor with similar sample sizes (~170). With roughly 57 patients per arm, the trial has very high power for an effect of this size, and the mechanism works independently of DPP-4 inhibition. The main residual risks are operational: a single site, possible enrollment shortfall or delay, or execution problems.

Kv7.2/7.3 opening is a validated mechanism in focal epilepsy: ezogabine was approved, and azetukalner was clearly positive in both Phase 2b and Phase 3. Adjunctive focal-seizure trials of mechanistically sound drugs against placebo succeed fairly often, and the 75 mg open-label responder data are encouraging. Against that, BHV-7000 has no controlled focal efficacy data, it failed its primary endpoints in MDD and bipolar mania, and its selective low-sedation profile may mean weaker target engagement than azetukalner. Biohaven's late-stage track record is spotty and Part B's sample size is modest, so I land moderately above even odds.

The efficacy signal comes only from a post hoc subgroup of a failed Phase 2a cognition trial, measured on the NPI rather than the CMAI. Every other 5-HT6 antagonist has failed in Alzheimer's, and CMAI agitation trials show large placebo responses, with even approved or promising drugs such as brexpiprazole and AXS-05 producing mixed results. The DSMB's decision not to raise the sample size and the over-enrollment add little information. Two dose arms give the trial two chances to hit significance, which lifts the estimate slightly, but a probability of roughly 25% seems appropriate.

Stapokibart already succeeded in an adult phase 3 SAR trial (PHECDA, n=108) on the same 2-week rTNSS primary endpoint, with a clear effect (−1.3, P=0.0008), and this adolescent extension uses a similar design with a slightly larger sample (n=136). Uncertainties remain: the registration lists no eosinophil ≥300 enrichment, and the phase 2 MERAK missed this endpoint in an unselected population. Enrollment is also compressed into a short autumn pollen window, and seasonal symptom trials are vulnerable to variable pollen loads and high placebo response. Extrapolation trials of a proven drug usually succeed, but these risks pull the estimate down to about 70%.

177Lu-DOTATATE has repeatedly and strongly beaten octreotide LAR 60 mg on PFS in this population (NETTER-1 HR 0.21, 20-month PFS 65% vs 11%; NETTER-2 HR 0.28), and a Chinese monotherapy analogue (XT-XTR008) also met its PFS endpoint against the same comparator. With n=184 and a weak control arm, even a much smaller effect than NETTER-1's, such as an 18-month PFS gap of about 25 points, should be readily detectable. The main risks are execution and operational: a single site, an open-label design with no DMC, a likely slipping timeline, an unclear powering and analysis plan, and possible product or quality differences for this generic-style radioligand.

ECLIPSE 1 showed 79% undetectable HDV RNA with tobevibart+elebsiran versus 0% in untreated controls, and SOLSTICE showed about 41% TND at week 24. The control here is continued bulevirtide in patients who have already failed to suppress on it, so its week-24 TND rate should be near zero. With about 150 patients randomized, even a 25–35% response in the combination arm against roughly 0–5% on bulevirtide would be highly significant. The main risks are lower efficacy in this pretreated population, a different endpoint definition (TND rather than <LLOQ), or a non-standard analysis, but overall success looks very likely.

This trial tests an oral SERD as monotherapy against fulvestrant in an all-comer population that was not selected for ESR1 mutation. In that setting the class record is mixed: EMERALD and the phase 2 SERENA-2 were positive, while EMBER-3 (imlunestrant), acelERA (giredestrant) and AMEERA-3 were negative overall, and a pooled HR of 0.80 had a confidence interval crossing 1. Patients here have had only 1–2 prior endocrine lines and many Chinese patients may not have had a CDK4/6 inhibitor, so ESR1 mutations will be less common and fulvestrant 500 mg should perform relatively well, shrinking the expected benefit. Working in D-0502's favour are the large 640-patient sample and the sponsor's choice to run a registrational trial, but there are no randomized data for the drug and its single-agent activity is uncertain.
